result.summary: The Galati attack a temple near Trachis and are beaten, then Brennus sends a large force under Orestorius and Combutis into Ætolia, where they commit atrocities at Callion before the Ætolians punish them. Meanwhile Brennus crosses Mount Œta by the Ænianes' path, routs the Phocian guards in a mist, and forces the Greeks to evacuate Thermopylæ by Athenian ships.

scenes.title: Repulse near Trachis
scenes.summary: Galati try to cross Œta and plunder Athene's temple, but Telesarchus' garrison defeats them. Brennus then plans to draw the Ætolians home.
scenes.stakes: The Greek garrison risks death defending the temple and pass; Telesarchus is killed.

scenes.title: Atrocities at Callion
scenes.summary: Orestorius and Combutis lead picked troops into Ætolia and sack Callion with horrible cruelty.
scenes.stakes: The people of Callion face slaughter, outrage and death.

scenes.title: Ætolian vengeance
scenes.summary: The Ætolians, men and women, rush home and harass the retreating Galati, killing half of them.
scenes.stakes: The Ætolians must save their remaining towns from the same fate.

scenes.title: Brennus turns Thermopylæ
scenes.summary: Guided by the Ænianes and Heraclea's people, Brennus crosses Œta in a mist and routs the Phocians. The Athenians evacuate the Greeks by ship.
scenes.stakes: The Greek army risks being surrounded and destroyed.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses Galati and Celts for the same Gallic invaders.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias cites Pindar on how people ignore others' misfortunes while oppressed by their own.

analysis.text: The passage contrasts barbarian cruelty with Greek resistance, and shows how self-interest, like that of the Ænianes, can betray a common cause.
It describes the Gallic invasion of Greece in 279 BC, which ended the Thermopylæ defence much as the Persian flanking path had earlier.

language_notes.text: Galati is Pausanias' name for the Gauls (Celts) who invaded Greece in 279 BC; the Greeks also call them Celts.
Refers to the Odyssey, where the Læstrygones and the Cyclops devour Ulysses' men; Pausanias says Callion's horrors make such tales seem believable.
Hydarnes the Mede led Persians over the mountain path in 480 BC, betraying Leonidas' Spartans at Thermopylæ (Herodotus).
Pindar, the Greek lyric poet, is cited for a proverb about selfishness; the exact lines are not given.
"Close quarters" means hand-to-hand fighting at short range.
Triremes were warships with three banks of oars; here they serve as transports.

context_notes.text: Trachis and Heraclea lay near Thermopylæ, the narrow coastal pass between Mount Œta and the sea, the classic defensive line of central Greece.
Brennus was the Galatian leader of this invasion; he hoped to divide the Greek allies by threatening Ætolia.
Patræ was a city of Achæa in the northern Peloponnese; Pausanias stresses that only its people came to help the Ætolians.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks in his own person, using his wide reading to judge the atrocities as exceeding anything he has heard.
Youths, old men and women all joining the fight shows Ætolian unity and fury, heightening the contrast with the barbarians' cruelty.
The Ænianes' self-interested betrayal is capped by a proverb, ironically excusing a choice that endangers all Greece.
The mist hiding the sun suggests fate turning against the Greeks, and echoes the earlier Persian betrayal at the same pass.
